LINGLING WEI   TAICHUNG, Taiwan—The first course arrived on a miniature lacquered rack, the kind you’d expect to hold ink brushes in a scholar’s studio. Instead, eight scallion stalks hung from it, carved and lashed with red thread down to the tapered tips. Below, on a plain white plate, sat the actual dish: shrimp nested in crisp cups.

   Our local host narrated what followed with the ease of a docent: yellow croaker steamed in fragrant rice wine and a whole fruitwood-roasted duck, brought out intact before being carved three ways tableside. 

   It took me a moment to realize why the meal left me a little dazed. Every element—the reverence for ingredients and the literary references baked into the plating—was unmistakably, deeply Chinese. And yet I was in Taichung, in central Taiwan, not Beijing or Shanghai, eating what may have been the most culturally fluent high-end Chinese meal of my life, on the island the mainland insists isn’t really its own country.

   That’s the thing about the Taiwan-versus-mainland food comparison many people reach for. Oil, seasoning and Japanese colonial influence make Taiwanese cooking lighter than its mainland counterpart. But the divergence that stayed with me isn’t what is on the plate but what the plate is trying to say. Taiwan and the mainland share a common Chinese cultural heritage. Taiwan more often treats it as something to enjoy than something to display, prove or broadcast.

What I ate in Taichung was neither. 

   The scallion-brush presentation only works if the kitchen and the diner are both already in on it. The enjoyment is in not needing to explain the reference, or oversell the moment.

   It’s a small sample—one trip, and a dozen meals, and a mainland I’m remembering as much as reporting on. But the instinct kept showing up wherever I looked. At a mid-range seafood restaurant in Taipei, packed with locals under swirling orange artwork, a squat robot server rolled between the tables ferrying dishes. Nobody looked up. Instead of being a novelty, it was simply absorbed into the rhythm of the room. 

   Compare that to the mainland, where the robot waiter reaches me the way it’s built to: a viral clip and a “look how advanced we are” flex. Technology is used as spectacle as much as a tool.

   Then there’s portion size. At a casual spot in downtown Taipei, the tables around me were ordering like people who meant to finish—a few dishes, no more. I did the same: three dishes for lunch on my own, a whole fried fish in a sweet-tart sauce, braised pork in a clay pot, and tofu in a sizzling skillet. I expected to leave stuffed. I didn’t. The portions were sized for pleasure, not a food-coma dare. I finished everything and still stood up afterward.

   Set those scenes side by side and Taiwan’s food culture treats tradition, tech and abundance as things that exist for the diner’s pleasure. Nothing is enlisted to make a larger point about civilizational greatness.

Taiwan seems to have kept an older, calmer relationship to its own culinary inheritance. 

   It’s the same pattern I found this summer in Taiwan’s temples, thick with incense and unbothered worshippers, versus the mainland faith largely dismantled in the Cultural Revolution and revived only under the party’s careful management. (That’s a subject I’ll return to later, in another part of The Wall Street Journal.)

   Left alone, tradition gets sillier and more alive whether it involves a god, a robot, or a scallion masquerading as a paintbrush.

A Food Crawl in Taiwan Finds Chinese Tradition Without the Spectacle
 
Plus, China rejects claims it could have warned Nepal earlier of deadly floods and how China weathered the Iran oil shock, in charts
 
 
Lunch for one—author Lingling Wei—in Taipei. LINGLING WEI
 

TAICHUNG, Taiwan—The first course arrived on a miniature lacquered rack, the kind you’d expect to hold ink brushes in a scholar’s studio. Instead, eight scallion stalks hung from it, carved and lashed with red thread down to the tapered tips. Below, on a plain white plate, sat the actual dish: shrimp nested in crisp cups.

 

Our local host narrated what followed with the ease of a docent: yellow croaker steamed in fragrant rice wine and a whole fruitwood-roasted duck, brought out intact before being carved three ways tableside. 

 

It took me a moment to realize why the meal left me a little dazed. Every element—the reverence for ingredients and the literary references baked into the plating—was unmistakably, deeply Chinese. And yet I was in Taichung, in central Taiwan, not Beijing or Shanghai, eating what may have been the most culturally fluent high-end Chinese meal of my life, on the island the mainland insists isn’t really its own country.

 

That’s the thing about the Taiwan-versus-mainland food comparison many people reach for. Oil, seasoning and Japanese colonial influence make Taiwanese cooking lighter than its mainland counterpart. But the divergence that stayed with me isn’t what is on the plate but what the plate is trying to say. Taiwan and the mainland share a common Chinese cultural heritage. Taiwan more often treats it as something to enjoy than something to display, prove or broadcast.

On the mainland, where I grew up, elaborate dining often pulls toward two poles: stiff banquet formality, heavy on baijiu-fueled toasts to whoever outranks you, or “Chinese fine dining” that’s really French-style tasting menu mixed with local ingredients. What I ate in Taichung was neither. 

 

The scallion-brush presentation only works if the kitchen and the diner are both already in on it. The enjoyment is in not needing to explain the reference, or oversell the moment.

 

It’s a small sample—one trip, and a dozen meals, and a mainland I’m remembering as much as reporting on. But the instinct kept showing up wherever I looked. At a mid-range seafood restaurant in Taipei, packed with locals under swirling orange artwork, a squat robot server rolled between the tables ferrying dishes. Nobody looked up. Instead of being a novelty, it was simply absorbed into the rhythm of the room. 

 

Compare that to the mainland, where the robot waiter reaches me the way it’s built to: a viral clip and a “look how advanced we are” flex. Technology is used as spectacle as much as a tool.

 

Then there’s portion size. At a casual spot in downtown Taipei, the tables around me were ordering like people who meant to finish—a few dishes, no more. I did the same: three dishes for lunch on my own, a whole fried fish in a sweet-tart sauce, braised pork in a clay pot, and tofu in a sizzling skillet. I expected to leave stuffed. I didn’t. The portions were sized for pleasure, not a food-coma dare. I finished everything and still stood up afterward.

 

On the mainland, the Communist Party has a campaign against food waste. Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, has twice backed 光盘行动, or the “Clean Plate” campaign that has restaurants urging guests to order one dish fewer than their headcount. In Taiwan, the plate just arrives meant to be finished.

 

Set those scenes side by side and Taiwan’s food culture treats tradition, tech and abundance as things that exist for the diner’s pleasure. Nothing is enlisted to make a larger point about civilizational greatness. 

 

A mainland version of Chinese culture, at least in the banquets and buildings I grew up around, often needed official sanction before tradition could be revived and modernity needed to be broadcast to count. Taiwan seems to have kept an older, calmer relationship to its own culinary inheritance. 

 

It’s the same pattern I found this summer in Taiwan’s temples, thick with incense and unbothered worshippers, versus the mainland faith largely dismantled in the Cultural Revolution and revived only under the party’s careful management. (That’s a subject I’ll return to later, in another part of The Wall Street Journal.)

 

Left alone, tradition gets sillier and more alive whether it involves a god, a robot, or a scallion masquerading as a paintbrush.

 

What stands out to you about how tradition is treated in Taiwan or China? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com. Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in an upcoming issue (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

 

This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

China in a Few Headlines

 

• China’s 1-billion-plus-barrel oil stockpile has cushioned the Iran crisis and capped global prices, though related export limits are hurting domestic refineries.

 

• Ahead of their Monday meeting in Kyrgyzstan, a Russia increasingly dependent on China leaves Putin in a junior role to Xi, who gains cheap oil and market dominance.

 

• Taiwan’s legislature approved a $7 billion six-year plan to build a military drone supply chain free of Chinese components to deter a potential attack by China.

 
 
 

The Number

 
3,000
 

Following a massive flood in northern Nepal and Tibet that left over 3,000 missing, China rejected claims that it could have provided Nepal with earlier warning of the deadly disaster.
